lesson.title: Harmonic Distortion: When a Circuit Adds Notes You Didn't Play
lesson.summary: Harmonic distortion occurs when a circuit's nonlinearity adds unwanted energy at integer multiples of an input signal's frequency, coloring the original tone with extra overtones that were never part of the original signal.
lesson.body:
An ideal, perfectly linear circuit produces an output that is simply a scaled, and possibly inverted or shifted, copy of whatever went into it, containing only the frequency or frequencies that were actually fed in. Real circuits are never perfectly linear. Transistors, op-amps pushed near their limits, transformers, and speaker drivers all deviate somewhat from a perfectly straight input to output relationship. When you drive a nonlinear circuit with a single pure tone, its fundamental frequency, the output is no longer a clean copy at just that one frequency. It also contains energy at twice that frequency, called the second harmonic, three times that frequency, the third harmonic, and so on. These are exactly the same integer multiple, overtone relationships you already know from the harmonics concept, just now generated unintentionally by an imperfect circuit rather than being part of the original musical source.

Different shapes of nonlinearity tend to favor different harmonic orders. Nonlinearities that are asymmetric, treating positive and negative swings of the signal differently, tend to generate more even order harmonics, while symmetric nonlinearities tend to favor odd order harmonics. You will see this distinction matter again once clipping is covered later in this sequence.

Here is a worked example. Suppose a 1 kHz fundamental tone with an amplitude of 1 V is driven into a mildly nonlinear amplifier stage, and the output also contains a second harmonic at 2 kHz with an amplitude of 0.02 V. Expressed relative to the fundamental in decibels: 20 times log10(0.02 divided by 1). Since 0.02 divided by 1 is just 0.02, and log10(0.02) equals log10(2) minus 2, which is 0.301 minus 2, or negative 1.699, multiplying by 20 gives about negative 33.98 dB. In plain percentage terms, that second harmonic sits at about 2 percent of the fundamental's amplitude.

Real nonlinear circuits rarely produce just one isolated harmonic. They typically generate a whole series at once, a second harmonic, a third, a fourth, each at its own level. The next chapter shows how to combine an entire series of harmonics like that into a single, standard percentage figure.
